unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brackenhill Home Furnishings is a private limited company based in Country X founded in 2014. It operates 3 stores in the capital city, employing 64 staff, and sells sofas, dining tables and bedroom furniture at mid-market prices. It hopes to capture rising demand from first-time buyers and families moving house. Last year revenue was $8.6 million, up from $7.4 million a year earlier.

The Country X economy has been in the growth stage of the business cycle for 2 years, with unemployment falling to 5% and consumer spending rising. To keep growth going, the government is considering cutting income tax from 22% to 19%. The directors must decide whether to open a fourth store in the southern suburbs at a cost of $1.2 million, or hold the money in reserve in case the economy slows.

questions.question_text: Define 'business cycle'.
questions.model_answer: The business cycle is the regular pattern of fluctuations (ups and downs) in economic activity over time, typically moving through stages such as growth, boom, recession and slump. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the regular pattern/cycle of fluctuations in economic activity over time
Names at least two stages, e.g. growth, boom, recession, slump

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenhill Home Furnishings' revenue rose.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer spending rises during the growth stage of the business cycle, so households are more willing to buy big items such as sofas and dining tables. [k] This is shown by revenue rising from $7.4 million to $8.6 million. [app] Reason 2: Unemployment has fallen to 5%, so more people have jobs and disposable income, and can afford mid-market furniture; rising demand explains why the directors are considering a fourth store. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that consumer spending/demand rises in the growth stage
Identifies that lower unemployment increases consumer incomes/spending power
application_max_2: Links rising spending to revenue growth from $7.4 million to $8.6 million
Links 5% unemployment / growth stage to mid-market furniture demand and the fourth store plan

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brackenhill Home Furnishings might face if it opens the fourth store in the southern suburbs.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The new store costs $1.2 million, so cash reserves would be greatly reduced and the firm may need to borrow, adding extra costs to the business. [k] With revenue of $8.6 million, spending $1.2 million is a large commitment that could strain cash if sales disappoint. [app] The extra fixed costs of rent and wages for a fourth outlet must be covered before profit rises, so profit could fall in the short term. [an] Problem 2: Opening in the southern suburbs is risky if the economy slows; a growth stage can end in a boom followed by a recession or slump. [k] The 3 stores already employ 64 staff, and a fourth store would add more staff and costs before demand in the suburbs is proven. [app] If income tax is not cut from 22% to 19% as hoped, consumer spending could weaken and the new store could make losses. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the financial strain/cash flow risk of a $1.2 million outlay
Identifies that the growth stage could end and demand could fall
application_max_2: References the $1.2 million cost against $8.6 million revenue
References 64 staff, the 3 stores, or the 22% to 19% tax cut uncertainty
analysis_max_2: Explains how extra fixed costs reduce profit in the short term (cost coverage logic)
Explains the link between the business cycle turning down and the new store becoming loss-making

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenhill Home Furnishings should open the fourth store now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, opening now lets Brackenhill Home Furnishings capture demand in the growth stage, when consumer spending is rising and unemployment is just 5%. [k] Revenue has already risen from $7.4 million to $8.6 million, showing strong demand for the sofas and furniture the new store would sell. [app] A fourth store in the southern suburbs would widen the customer base, spread fixed costs over more sales and raise profit further. [an] However, the fourth store would cost $1.2 million, and the growth stage can turn into a boom followed by a slowdown. [k] If income tax is not cut from 22% to 19%, or the economy slows, the new store's wages and rent would still need paying and the money held in reserve would be gone. [app] Keeping the cash in reserve would protect the 64 staff's wages and the existing 3 stores if the cycle turned down, but it would mean losing sales to competitors that expand first. [an] Overall, the firm should open the fourth store, but only once the income tax cut is confirmed, because acting on strong demand now gains a first-mover advantage while the condition limits the risk to cash flow. [eval] This is justified by the rise in revenue from $7.4 million to $8.6 million; spending $1.2 million is safer once demand and government policy are both confirmed. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that the growth stage supports expansion (rising demand, low unemployment)
Identifies the risk that the cycle turns down / growth becomes a slowdown
application_max_2: References revenue rising from $7.4 million to $8.6 million and 5% unemployment
References the $1.2 million cost, the 22% to 19% tax cut and 64 staff / 3 stores
analysis_max_2: Explains how a new store spreads fixed costs and raises profit (expansion benefit)
Explains how reserve cash protects the business if the cycle turns down (risk analysis)
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement with a stated condition or priority
Weighs expansion benefits against downturn risk rather than arguing one side only

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppermere Brick and Cement Co is a public limited company in Country X operating 2 plants that supply clay bricks and ready-mix cement to customers nationwide. It supplies bricks mainly to house-builders and large housing developers. It employs 180 workers and produced 9.5 million bricks last year. Revenue rose to $14.2 million from $11.8 million the previous year. Orders are at record levels and the order book is full for the next 12 months.

The Country X economy is in a boom, with GDP growing by 4.5% a year and the construction sector expanding. The government is considering raising corporation tax from 24% to 28% to cool the economy. The board must decide whether to invest $3 million in a third plant to meet demand, or delay expansion until the boom ends.

questions.question_text: Define 'boom'.
questions.model_answer: A boom is the peak stage of the business cycle, when economic activity is at its highest, demand is strong, output is high and unemployment is low. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the boom as the peak/high point of the business cycle
Identifies high demand, output or employment / strong economic activity

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of a boom on Coppermere Brick and Cement Co.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Demand for bricks and cement rises sharply in a boom, so the firm sells more and revenue grows; it produced 9.5 million bricks and revenue reached $14.2 million. [k] [app] Effect 2: In a boom labour is scarce and wages tend to rise, so keeping 180 workers paid may squeeze margins even as sales increase and the order book stays full. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that demand/output rise in a boom
Identifies that labour is scarce / wages rise in a boom
application_max_2: References 9.5 million bricks and/or revenue of $14.2 million
References 180 workers, the full order book or the construction sector expansion

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of investing $3 million in a new third plant during the boom.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Construction costs and wages are high in a boom, so the $3 million budget could overrun and the firm may need to borrow more. [k] With revenue of $14.2 million, extra borrowing at this point would still cut profit, especially if corporation tax rises from 24% to 28%. [app] Higher fixed costs from a third plant must be paid even if orders fall, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes more fragile. [an] Problem 2: When the boom ends, demand for bricks falls; a new plant built now may be underused, leaving excess capacity and heavy fixed costs. [k] Orders are full for the next 12 months, but the business cycle will eventually move into a slowdown, and the extra workers taken on cannot be avoided easily. [app] Underused capacity spreads fixed costs over fewer bricks, raising average costs and reducing competitiveness. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that costs are high in a boom / the budget may overrun
Identifies that demand will fall when the boom ends, leaving excess capacity
application_max_2: References the $3 million cost against $14.2 million revenue or the 24% to 28% tax rise
References the full 12-month order book or the boom eventually ending
analysis_max_2: Explains that higher fixed costs raise the break-even point and fragile profit
Explains that underused capacity raises average cost per brick (diseconomy/under-absorption)

questions.question_text: Do you think Coppermere Brick and Cement Co should invest $3 million in a third plant now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: in a boom, demand is strong and delaying expansion means losing orders to rivals. [k] Revenue has already climbed from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the order book is full for 12 months, so more capacity is needed urgently. [app] A third plant would let the firm serve all its housing-developer customers and raise profit despite the possible rise in corporation tax from 24% to 28%. [an] However, booms do not last forever; the business cycle will eventually turn to a downturn. [k] If the economy slows after the boom, the third plant's $3 million cost and the wages of extra workers would leave the firm with excess capacity and weaker cash to pay its 180 workers. [app] Delaying expansion until the boom ends would reduce this risk but would hand orders to competitors at the peak of demand. [an] Overall, the board should invest in the third plant now but phase the building over 18 to 24 months, keeping a cash reserve in case the cycle turns, because the revenue evidence strongly justifies expansion. [eval] This is justified by the $2.4 million revenue increase and the full order book; phasing the spend limits the damage if the boom ends sooner than expected. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies strong demand / capacity shortage in a boom
Identifies that the boom will end and demand will fall (cycle risk)
application_max_2: References revenue growth from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the full order book
References the $3 million cost, 180 workers or the 24% to 28% corporation tax rise
analysis_max_2: Explains how extra capacity raises profit when demand is strong
Explains how excess capacity and fixed costs hurt the firm after the boom
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. invest now but phase it)
Weighs opportunity cost of delay against the risk of over-expansion

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches is a partnership in Country X selling luxury watches and jewellery from 2 boutiques. It employs 14 specialist sales staff. Average takings per boutique fell to $95,000 a month in the latest quarter, down from $130,000 a year earlier, as Country X entered a slump. Footfall has fallen by a third since the slump began, and two nearby luxury retailers have closed.

Consumer confidence is very low and sales of luxury goods have dropped sharply. To help the economy, the government has cut VAT from 20% to 15% for 12 months. The partners must decide whether to cut prices by 10% to attract cautious buyers, or keep prices unchanged to protect the exclusive image of the brand.

questions.question_text: Define 'slump'.
questions.model_answer: A slump is the lowest point of the business cycle, when economic activity, output, incomes and employment are at their weakest and consumer spending is very low. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the slump as the lowest/weakest stage of the business cycle
Identifies very low output, incomes, employment and/or consumer spending

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sales of luxury watches and jewellery fall during a slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In a slump, consumer incomes and confidence are very low, so households postpone non-essential high-price purchases such as luxury watches. [k] This is shown by takings per boutique falling from $130,000 to $95,000 a month. [app] Reason 2: In a slump, people fear for their jobs, so they prioritise essentials over luxury goods. [k] Footfall has fallen by a third and two nearby luxury retailers have closed, confirming the collapse in demand. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies low consumer incomes/confidence as the cause of weak luxury demand
Identifies job insecurity/fear of unemployment causing postponement of big non-essential purchases
application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 per boutique a month
References footfall falling by a third / two nearby luxury retailers closing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 10%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 10% price cut shrinks the profit margin on every watch sold, yet the boutiques still have to pay 14 specialist sales staff and rent. [k] Takings are already down to $95,000 per boutique a month, so lowering prices could erode profit further unless sales volume rises sharply. [app] Lower margins reduce the cash available to ride out the slump and could force staff hour cuts. [an] Problem 2: Heavy discounting can damage the exclusive brand image that convinces customers to pay high prices. [k] Keeping prices unchanged protects that exclusive image, but cutting prices by 10% may teach buyers to wait for discounts rather than pay full price. [app] If the exclusive image weakens, takings may never recover to $130,000 a month even when the slump ends. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut reduces profit margins per unit
Identifies that discounting damages an exclusive/premium brand image
application_max_2: References takings of $95,000 vs $130,000 or the 14 specialist sales staff
References the exclusive brand image / 10% discount
analysis_max_2: Explains the margin/volume trade-off and its effect on cash (staff cuts)
Explains how a weakened brand image undermines long-term takingsRecovery

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches should cut prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: No: cutting prices by 10% would shrink margins on all watches and risk destroying the exclusive brand image. [k] Takings per boutique have fallen from $130,000 to $95,000, but a 10% discount would erode what profit remains and encourage buyers to delay purchases. [app] The VAT cut from 20% to 15% already lowers shelf prices by about 4% if passed on, which stimulates demand without the firm cutting its own prices. [an] Yes: a 10% cut could attract cautious buyers who feel they are getting value, especially during the 12 months the VAT cut lasts. [k] Takings of $95,000 a month per boutique show demand is weak; a well-advertised 10% discount could clear slow-moving stock and draw customers back into the 2 boutiques. [app] More sales at lower margin could raise total profit if enough extra customers are attracted, but it is uncertain whether a slump can be discounted away. [an] Overall, the partners should keep headline prices unchanged and pass on the VAT cut instead of cutting prices by a full 10%, because protecting the brand and margin matters most for luxury goods in a slump. [eval] This is justified by the collapse in takings from $130,000 to $95,000; discounting heavily rarely restores luxury demand, so a modest VAT-linked saving is the safer move. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the margin/brand-image argument against a 10% price cut
Identifies the demand-stimulation argument in favour of a 10% price cut
application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 and the VAT cut from 20% to 15%
References the 2 boutiques, 12-month VAT window or footfall fall
analysis_max_2: Explains the VAT pass-on as a softer demand stimulus (roughly 4% shelf-price fall)
Explains the margin/volume/brand trade-off and its effect on profit
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. keep prices, pass on VAT saving)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Harlan Building Materials Ltd is a private limited company in Country X supplying cement, sand and aggregates from 2 depots. It delivers to building firms, housing developers and public works contractors across the region. It employs 46 people and revenue was $6.8 million last year. In March the government announced a $250 million national road-building programme over 5 years.

Harlan has been invited to tender for a $4.5 million contract to supply cement to 3 road projects. Winning would require buying 2 new delivery trucks costing $380,000 each and hiring 12 more drivers, an investment of $760,000. The directors must decide whether to tender for the contract, or stay focused on their 140 regular small customers and avoid taking on debt.

questions.question_text: Define 'taxation'.
questions.model_answer: Taxation is the compulsory payment of money to the government by individuals and businesses, used to fund public spending and services. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies taxation as compulsory payments to the government
Identifies that taxes are used to fund public spending/services

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Harlan Building Materials Ltd of government spending on road-building.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Public spending creates direct orders for building materials, so Harlan can win lucrative contracts such as the $4.5 million tender for 3 road projects. [k] The $250 million programme over 5 years guarantees demand far beyond what small customers alone would provide. [app] Benefit 2: Better roads improve distribution across the region, making deliveries from Harlan's 2 depots faster and cheaper and opening access to new customers. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that government spending creates direct demand/contracts for materials
Identifies that better infrastructure lowers distribution costs or widens markets
application_max_2: References the $4.5 million tender / 3 road projects / $250 million, 5-year programme
References the 2 depots or the 140 regular customers context

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Harlan might face if it invests in the 2 new trucks and 12 drivers.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Buying 2 trucks at $380,000 each costs $760,000, a large sum for a firm with $6.8 million revenue that could strain cash or require borrowing. [k] If the $4.5 million contract is lost or delayed, the trucks and 12 more drivers would sit underused, raising average costs per delivery. [app] High fixed costs from trucks and wages must be covered even in quiet months, so profit could fall sharply. [an] Problem 2: Relying on one big government programme makes the firm vulnerable if budget cuts or delays reduce the road-building. [k] The programme runs over 5 years, and public spending can change with a new budget or a downturn in the business cycle. [app] If the contract ends, Harlan would still have the trucks and drivers to pay, and selling trucks is hard in a weak market. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/cash flow strain of buying trucks (or need to borrow)
Identifies dependence on government spending / risk the programme ends or is cut
application_max_2: References $380,000 per truck / $760,000 total against $6.8 million revenue
References the 5-year programme, the $4.5 million contract or the 12 extra drivers
analysis_max_2: Explains how fixed costs raise average cost per delivery when demand is weak
Explains how dependence on a single government programme raises business risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Harlan Building Materials Ltd should tender for the $4.5 million contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: winning the contract would transform Harlan's scale and profitability. [k] Revenue is $6.8 million, so $4.5 million of work over 5 years is roughly two-thirds of a year's sales added steadily, backed by the $250 million national programme. [app] Spending $760,000 on 2 trucks and 12 drivers lets Harlan capture this growth and build a reputation for large public projects. [an] However, the investment is large relative to the business and depends on government spending continuing. [k] If the tender fails or the programme is delayed, the $760,000 spent on trucks would strain cash and leave extra drivers idle, while the 140 regular small customers could feel neglected. [app] Staying focused on small customers avoids this risk but means forgoing the fastest-growing source of revenue available. [an] Overall, Harlan should tender, but negotiate milestone payments and stage the truck purchases so cash flow is protected if work is delayed. [eval] This is justified by the scale of the $250 million programme; the opportunity outweighs the risk, provided contract terms are secured before spending. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the growth/scale opportunity from the $4.5 million contract
Identifies the risk of dependence on government spending / a failed tender
application_max_2: References $6.8 million revenue vs $4.5 million contract (two-thirds of a year's sales)
References the $760,000 investment, the $250 million programme or the 140 regular small customers
analysis_max_2: Explains how the contract spreads fixed costs and builds reputation/scale
Explains the cash-flow and neglect risk for existing customers if it fails
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. tender with milestone terms/staged spend)
Weighs growth opportunity against dependence on government policy

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Haver & Grey Electronics is a private limited company in Country X running 4 high-street shops selling TVs, laptops and washing machines. It has traded for 9 years and employs 52 staff. Revenue last year was $11.6 million, down from $12.9 million. The rise in tax was announced in the March budget.

To reduce a budget deficit, the government has raised income tax from 20% to 23% and VAT from 17.5% to 20%. The shops report fewer customers and average spend per transaction has fallen to $310 from $355. Footfall has been falling for 6 months. The directors must decide whether to cut prices by 5% to win sales back, or hold prices and wait for the government's promise of lower inflation.

questions.question_text: Identify two government economic objectives.
questions.model_answer: Two government economic objectives are: (1) economic growth; and (2) stable prices (low inflation). Other acceptable answers include full employment, balance of payments stability and redistribution of income. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Names any two government economic objectives (e.g. economic growth, full employment, stable prices, balance of payments, redistribution of income)
Accept equivalent wording, e.g. low unemployment or low prices/inflation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Haver & Grey Electronics' revenue has fallen.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher income tax from 20% to 23% reduces households' disposable income, so they cut back on big-ticket items such as TVs and washing machines. [k] This is shown by average spend per transaction falling from $355 to $310. [app] Reason 2: VAT has risen from 17.5% to 20%, pushing up prices in the shops and discouraging purchases; revenue has fallen from $12.9 million to $11.6 million across the 4 shops. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that higher income tax reduces disposable income and consumer spending
Identifies that higher VAT raises prices and reduces quantity demanded
application_max_2: References spend per transaction falling from $355 to $310 or the 20% to 23% income tax rise
References revenue falling from $12.9 million to $11.6 million or the 17.5% to 20% VAT rise / 4 shops

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 5%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 5% price cut reduces revenue per sale when spend per transaction has already fallen to $310, eroding retail margins. [k] On revenue of $11.6 million, a 5% cut removes about $580,000 of income unless volume rises sharply. [app] The fall is caused by higher taxes rather than high prices, so a price cut attacks the wrong problem and profit could fall below sustainable levels. [an] Problem 2: A price cut could start a price war; rivals may match the 5% cut, leaving all shops with lower margins and no extra market share. [k] With 4 shops and 52 staff to pay, Haver & Grey cannot absorb prolonged losses easily. [app] A price war risks damaging the shops' reputation and could force cost cuts that harm service and staff morale. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut squeezes revenue/margins
Identifies the risk of a price war / rivals matching the cut
application_max_2: References $310 spend per transaction or $11.6 million revenue / the 5% cut
References the 4 shops and 52 staff or the wrong-diagnosis point (taxes, not prices)
analysis_max_2: Explains the arithmetic: a 5% cut on $11.6 million removes about $580,000 unless volume rises
Explains why a cut cannot fix a demand fall caused by taxation (wrong instrument)

questions.question_text: Do you think Haver & Grey Electronics should cut prices by 5%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: No: cutting prices by 5% would sacrifice margins without fixing the real problem, which is reduced disposable income caused by higher taxes. [k] Spend per transaction has already fallen from $355 to $310 and VAT is now 20%, so a 5% cut would lower revenue further when sales have dropped from $12.9 million to $11.6 million. [app] Holding prices preserves the cash needed to pay the 52 staff and keeps the shops stocked; targeted promotions on slow lines are safer than an across-the-board cut. [an] Yes: a 5% cut could pull cautious households back into the 4 shops and rebuild footfall while rivals hold prices. [k] If the government delivers its promise of lower inflation, spending power recovers, and a visible discount now could make Haver & Grey the value destination in town. [app] More transactions at slightly lower margins could stabilise total profit, and winning customers now builds loyalty for the recovery. [an] Overall, the directors should not cut prices across the board by 5%; they should use targeted discounts and promotions instead, protecting margins while tempting back customers. [eval] This is justified because the fall in sales is caused by higher taxes and lower spending power, not by price perception, so a blanket cut would sacrifice profit for uncertain gain. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the argument against a cut (margin loss, wrong diagnosis)
Identifies the argument for a cut (stimulates demand, builds loyalty)
application_max_2: References spend falling from $355 to $310, VAT at 20% and revenue of $11.6 million/$12.9 million
References the 4 shops, 52 staff or the promise of lower inflation
analysis_max_2: Explains why a tax-driven demand fall is not cured by lowering prices (elasticity/diagnosis logic)
Explains how a cut could raise volume and loyalty enough to stabilise profit
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. targeted promotions instead of a 5% cut)
Weighs both sides using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Penny & Thread is a private limited company in Country X running 3 discount clothing stores in low-income areas. The stores sell own-brand clothing, school uniforms and household basics at very low prices for cash-strapped families. It employs 27 staff and revenue last year was $4.9 million.

As part of redistributing income, the government has increased weekly benefits for low-income families by $30 per child and cut the income tax rate for low-income households to 10%. Footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months, and shelves are emptying faster. The directors must decide whether to open a fourth store in a deprived estate at a cost of $600,000, or refurbish the existing 3 stores at a cost of $250,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'redistribution of income'.
questions.model_answer: Redistribution of income is the transfer of income from higher-income groups to lower-income groups, for example through taxes and benefits, to make the distribution of income more equal. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the transfer of income from richer to poorer groups
Identifies the mechanism (taxes and benefits) or the aim (greater equality)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the government's redistribution of income on Penny & Thread.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Low-income households have more money to spend, so demand for discount clothing rises; footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months. [k] [app] Effect 2: Higher benefits of $30 per child per week and an income tax rate of just 10% raise disposable income, increasing sales of own-brand clothing and school uniforms at low prices. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that benefits/lower tax raise disposable income of low-income households
Identifies that higher disposable income raises demand for goods and services
application_max_2: References the 12% rise in footfall / 3-month timeframe
References the $30 per child weekly benefit or the 10% income tax rate

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of refurbishing the existing 3 stores instead of opening a fourth.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Refurbishment at $250,000 costs less than half of the $600,000 needed for a new store, so the firm avoids heavy borrowing and keeps a cash cushion. [k] With revenue of only $4.9 million, committing $600,000 to an untested estate is a big financial risk. [app] Lower capital spending means lower financial risk and a quicker return on the investment, protecting profit and the 27 jobs. [an] Advantage 2: Upgrading the existing 3 stores keeps proven locations and customer bases while adding space and better displays to handle the 12% footfall rise. [k] The stores already sell own-brand clothing and uniforms that low-income families depend on, so improvements will directly serve current customers. [app] Refurbishment raises capacity where demand is already proven, so sales can rise with far less risk than opening in an untested estate. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the lower capital cost/risk of $250,000 vs $600,000
Identifies that existing stores have proven demand/customers
application_max_2: References $250,000 vs $600,000 and $4.9 million revenue
References the 12% footfall rise or the existing 3 stores selling own-brand clothing
analysis_max_2: Explains how lower capital spending reduces financial risk and protects cash/jobs
Explains that improving proven locations adds capacity with less risk than an untested site

questions.question_text: Do you think Penny & Thread should open the fourth store in the deprived estate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: opening the fourth store puts Penny & Thread directly in front of the low-income families who have just gained from the redistribution of income. [k] Benefits up by $30 per child per week, an income tax rate of just 10% and a 12% rise in footfall all point to durable demand that the existing 3 stores cannot absorb. [app] A fourth store in a deprived estate would capture this demand, spread fixed costs across 4 stores and lift revenue beyond $4.9 million. [an] However, the new store costs $600,000, more than twice the $250,000 refurbishment, and the benefit increase could be reduced in a future budget. [k] If demand falls back, the fourth store's rent and wages would burden the business, whereas refurbishing the existing 3 stores copes with growth at lower cost and lower risk. [app] Staying small protects the 27 staff and the proven customer base, but shelves are already emptying faster and customers may switch to rivals. [an] Overall, the directors should open the fourth store, because the 12% rise in footfall and the ongoing benefit increase justify expanding into underserved areas. [eval] This is justified by the demonstrated rise in low-income spending; staging the opening over 12 months would manage the risk of a future policy reversal. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the demand opportunity created by redistribution of income
Identifies the capital cost and policy-reversal risk of a fourth store
application_max_2: References the $30 per child benefit, 10% tax rate and 12% footfall rise
References the $600,000 vs $250,000 costs and $4.9 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Explains how a new store spreads fixed costs and lifts revenue beyond $4.9 million
Explains the risk/return trade-off of refurbishing vs opening if policy reverses
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. open now, staged over 12 months)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Meadowgate Grocers is a private limited company in Country X operating 5 neighbourhood supermarkets. Each store carries about 6,000 product lines and trades 7 days a week. It employs 88 staff and revenue was $16.4 million last year. Fresh food prices rose sharply this year and inflation reached 6%, above the government's target of stable prices at 2%. Suppliers are demanding higher prices for milk, bread and fresh produce.

The government is committed to restoring stable prices and has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively. Meadowgate's costs have risen 8%. The 6% figure would be the first across-the-board rise in 3 years. The directors must decide whether to raise shelf prices by 6% in line with inflation, or absorb the cost increase by cutting staff hours and promotions.

questions.question_text: Define 'stable prices'.
questions.model_answer: Stable prices means the general price level in the economy rises only slowly, i.e. inflation is low and predictable, so money keeps its value. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that the general price level rises only slowly (low inflation)
Identifies that prices are predictable / money keeps its value

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Meadowgate Grocers of inflation rising to 6%.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Supplier and wage costs rise — Meadowgate's costs have risen 8%, squeezing profit margins unless shelf prices go up; the firm is considering a 6% rise. [k] [app] Effect 2: Customers' purchasing power falls as prices rise, so shoppers become more price-sensitive and may switch to cheaper goods; with about 6,000 product lines to re-price, the workload and pressure on staff increase. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that inflation raises business costs/prices
Identifies that inflation erodes consumers' purchasing power and shifts demand
application_max_2: References the 8% rise in costs / the 6% price rise under consideration
References the 6,000 product lines or the 88 staff / $16.4 million revenue context

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of raising shelf prices by 6%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher prices may drive customers to discounters, reducing sales volume; with inflation already at 6%, a further rise could lose Meadowgate its price-sensitive shoppers. [k] Suppliers of milk, bread and fresh produce have raised prices by 8%, but passing on 6% of that still erodes margins while risking lower footfall across the 5 neighbourhood supermarkets. [app] Lower volumes would spread the 88 staff's wages over fewer sales, raising the average cost per transaction and squeezing profit. [an] Problem 2: Raising prices conflicts with the government's stable prices objective, and the government has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively; bad publicity could harm the brand. [k] The 6% rise would be the first across-the-board increase in 3 years, drawing customer attention to higher bills. [app] Reputational damage could outlast any short-term margin gain, especially if lower inflation arrives soon. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the risk of losing price-sensitive customers/sales volume
Identifies the conflict with the government's stable prices objective / reputational risk
application_max_2: References the 8% supplier cost rise vs the 6% proposed increase or the 5 supermarkets
References the 6,000 product lines, the 88 staff or the government's request
analysis_max_2: Explains the margin vs footfall trade-off (volume spread over fixed staff costs)
Explains how reputational damage can outweigh short-term margin gains

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowgate Grocers should raise prices by 6%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: with costs up 8%, not raising prices would wipe out margins and threaten the 88 jobs. [k] Revenue is $16.4 million and wages, rent and supplier costs are all rising with 6% inflation, so a 6% rise roughly tracks the market rather than exceeding it. [app] Raising prices protects the cash needed to stock about 6,000 product lines across 5 neighbourhood supermarkets, keeping service levels and staff hours intact. [an] However, the government wants stable prices at 2% and has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively, and customers already struggling with 6% inflation may shop elsewhere. [k] A 6% rise would be the first across-the-board increase in 3 years and could push price-sensitive shoppers to discounters, cutting volumes and revenue. [app] Absorbing costs by cutting staff hours and promotions protects headline prices but risks poorer service and lower morale among the 88 staff. [an] Overall, Meadowgate should raise prices by an average of 6% but keep staple items cheaper where possible, accepting slightly lower margins there to hold footfall. [eval] This is justified because fully absorbing an 8% cost rise would destroy profit, while a selective rise shares the burden fairly between the firm and its customers. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the margin-protection case for a price rise
Identifies the customer-loss/reputation risk and the stable prices objective tension
application_max_2: References the 8% cost rise vs the 6% proposed increase, $16.4 million revenue
References the 6,000 product lines, the 88 staff or the first rise in 3 years
analysis_max_2: Explains why inaction destroys margins (cost-price squeeze)
Explains the volume/margin trade-off across price-sensitive shoppers
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. selective 6% rise)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Larchmont Dairies is a private limited company in Country X producing butter and hard cheese. It buys milk from 38 local dairy farms and churns 6 days a week. It employs 96 workers at one creamery and sells mainly to supermarkets at home, and its main export is hard cheese. Last year it exported $2.1 million of cheese, double the $1.05 million exported the previous year.

The government wants to improve the balance of payments and is offering a 15% export grant for 3 years, and has imposed an 18% tariff on imported cheese. The directors must decide whether to build a second production line costing $2.8 million to expand exports, or focus on the domestic market, where the tariff on imports should lift their sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'balance of payments'.
questions.model_answer: The balance of payments is a record of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world over a period of time, including exports and imports of goods and services. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the balance of payments as a record of transactions with the rest of the world
Identifies that it includes exports and imports of goods and services

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Larchmont Dairies of exporting more cheese.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Export sales earn foreign currency for the country, directly supporting the government's balance of payments objective; Larchmont's exports rose to $2.1 million from $1.05 million. [k] [app] Benefit 2: Exporting spreads risk — selling abroad reduces reliance on the home market, so an economic downturn in Country X would not wipe out sales at the single creamery. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that exports earn foreign currency/support the balance of payments
Identifies that exporting spreads risk/reduces dependence on the home market
application_max_2: References exports doubling from $1.05 million to $2.1 million
References the single creamery / 96 workers / 38 local dairy farms context

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of building a second production line costing $2.8 million.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $2.8 million investment is large for one creamery employing 96 workers and may require borrowing, increasing financial risk. [k] If export demand disappoints, the new line may run below capacity, raising average costs and cutting profit. [app] High fixed costs would weigh on the firm even in quiet months, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes less secure. [an] Problem 2: Export markets are uncertain — exchange rate changes, transport costs and foreign competition can all squeeze margins. [k] The 15% export grant lasts only 3 years, and the 18% tariff on imported cheese could change in a future trade deal. [app] If the grant is withdrawn or the tariff is cut, the second line could become unprofitable and the firm would be left with surplus capacity. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/financial risk of a $2.8 million investment
Identifies export-market uncertainty (demand, exchange rates, foreign competition)
application_max_2: References the $2.8 million cost / 96 workers / one creamery
References the 15% grant ending after 3 years or the 18% tariff changing
analysis_max_2: Explains how underused capacity raises average costs and the break-even point
Explains how dependence on government policy (grant/tariff) threatens line profitability

questions.question_text: Do you think Larchmont Dairies should build the second production line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: doubling exports to $2.1 million proves the overseas market and aligns with the government's balance of payments priority. [k] The 15% export grant for 3 years, plus the 18% tariff on imported cheese, gives Larchmont both an export boost and home-market protection. [app] A $2.8 million second line could double capacity at the single creamery, lifting export revenue and profit while helping the national economy. [an] However, $2.8 million is a major commitment for a firm employing 96 workers, and export demand can shift with exchange rates and foreign competition. [k] If the grant ends after 3 years or the 18% tariff is cut in a trade deal, export margins could shrink and the line could be underused. [app] Focusing on the home market would capture the tariff benefit immediately with no new borrowing, but would cap growth at current export levels. [an] Overall, Larchmont should build the second line, phased over 18 months with the grant secured first, because export momentum from $1.05 million to $2.1 million justifies expanding capacity. [eval] This is justified by the government's 15% grant and the proven doubling of exports; phasing construction protects cash if export growth slows. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the growth case for export expansion and the grant support
Identifies the risks of dependence on the grant/tariff and export-market volatility
application_max_2: References exports doubling from $1.05 million to $2.1 million, the 15% grant
References the $2.8 million cost, 96 workers, the 18% tariff or 3-year grant period
analysis_max_2: Explains how the grant and tariff improve export economics and home-market protection
Explains how policy changes or demand shifts would make the line unprofitable
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. build, phased, grant secured first)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bluebell Catering Co is a private limited company in Country X providing school meals to 34 state schools in the capital. It cooks meals on-site and delivers to secondary schools. It employs 120 staff, including 45 kitchen assistants and 30 supervisors. Its school contract is worth $2.6 million a year, about 60% of revenue, which was $4.3 million last year. Staff costs are 65% of the contract price.

The government has announced cuts to education spending to reduce the budget deficit, cutting school catering budgets by 10% nationwide. The renewed contract would run for 3 years. Bluebell must decide whether to tender for the renewed contract at a 10% lower price, or move into corporate office catering, which would need $900,000 of new kitchen equipment.

questions.question_text: Define 'government spending'.
questions.model_answer: Government spending is money spent by the government on public goods and services, such as schools, hospitals, roads, welfare benefits and defence. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies government spending as money spent by the state on goods and services
Gives examples such as education, health, infrastructure or welfare benefits

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Bluebell Catering Co of the 10% cut in school catering budgets.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: The renewed contract price falls — a 10% cut on $2.6 million is about $260,000 a year of lost revenue. [k] [app] Effect 2: Bluebell must cut costs, for example by reducing the hours of the 45 kitchen assistants, which could lower morale and the quality of meals served to the 34 state schools. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a 10% budget cut lowers government contract prices/revenue
Identifies that firms must reduce costs (staff, ingredients) to cope
application_max_2: References the 10% cut and/or the $2.6 million contract (about $260,000 a year)
References the 45 kitchen assistants / 34 state schools / 120 staff

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of moving into corporate office catering.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Corporate clients are not affected by government education cuts, so revenue becomes more stable; Bluebell would be far less exposed if school budgets are cut again when the renewed 3-year contract ends. [k] Corporate meals would be sold at market rates, helping replace some of the $2.6 million school income. [app] Stable, higher-margin contracts would support the profit needed to pay the 120 staff and grow the business. [an] Benefit 2: Diversifying into offices and factories spreads risk and reduces dependence on a single government customer worth about 60% of revenue. [k] Winning new private clients would reduce reliance on political decisions made in each budget. [app] A broader customer base makes revenue more predictable and improves the firm's bargaining position with suppliers. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that corporate clients are unaffected by government budget cuts (stable demand)
Identifies that diversifying reduces dependence on one customer/sector
application_max_2: References the $2.6 million contract / 60% of revenue / $4.3 million revenue
References the 3-year contract, the 10% cut or the 120 staff
analysis_max_2: Explains how corporate income stabilises cash flow and supports wages/growth
Explains the risk-spreading benefit of a broader customer base

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluebell Catering Co should move into corporate office catering? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: corporate catering frees Bluebell from budget cuts driven by government spending decisions, which have just fallen by 10%. [k] The school contract is worth $2.6 million, about 60% of revenue, so Bluebell is dangerously dependent on the government; diversifying spreads this risk. [app] Corporate clients would pay market rates instead of 10%-cut prices, lifting profit to support the 120 staff and the $4.3 million revenue base. [an] However, moving into corporate catering needs $900,000 of new kitchen equipment and Bluebell has no track record there. [k] Tendering for the renewed school contract at a 10% lower price keeps $2.6 million of income for 3 years and protects all 120 jobs, albeit at lower margins — a safer short-term option. [app] Corporate catering takes time to win, and if contracts are slow to arrive the firm could face a cash gap while paying for the new equipment. [an] Overall, Bluebell should move into corporate office catering in stages — keep the school contract and invest the $900,000 gradually as corporate orders grow. [eval] This is justified because it protects the existing 60% of revenue while reducing long-term dependence on government policy, balancing security with diversification. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the diversification/risk-reduction benefit of corporate catering
Identifies the cost and unproven-market risk ($900,000, no track record)
application_max_2: References the $2.6 million contract / 60% of revenue / $4.3 million revenue
References the 10% cut, the $900,000 equipment need, 3 years or 120 staff
analysis_max_2: Explains how corporate income replaces government-dependent revenue and stabilises profit
Explains the cash-flow risk of investing before corporate contracts are won
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. staged move keeping the school contract)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Harwick Appliances Ltd is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing washing machines and ovens. It sells to retailers, builders' merchants and export customers in 6 countries, and employs 210 workers at one factory. Revenue was $18.5 million last year, up from $16.1 million the year before. Wages have risen 7% this year.

The economy is close to full employment and the government has raised corporation tax from 21% to 25% to fund public spending. Harwick cannot recruit enough skilled assembly workers. The directors must decide whether to spend $1.5 million on automating 2 production lines, or keep the manual lines and accept slower output and rising labour costs. The 2 automated lines would cut the need for 30 assembly workers.

questions.question_text: Define 'full employment'.
questions.model_answer: Full employment is a situation in which everyone who is willing and able to work at the prevailing wage rate can find a job, i.e. unemployment is kept at a very low level. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that everyone willing and able to work can find a job
Identifies that unemployment is kept very low

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Harwick Appliances Ltd of the economy being close to full employment.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Skilled assembly workers are hard to find, so Harwick cannot recruit the workers it needs and output cannot grow; it already employs 210 workers at one factory. [k] [app] Effect 2: Wages across the economy are rising fast — Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year — pushing up costs and squeezing profit after the 25% corporation tax. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies labour shortages/recruitment difficulty near full employment
Identifies upward pressure on wages (and costs)
application_max_2: References 210 workers at one factory / inability to recruit assembly workers
References the 7% wage rise or the 25% corporation tax

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of automating the 2 production lines at a cost of $1.5 million.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $1.5 million investment must come from profit or borrowing, so cash is tied up and financial risk rises. [k] With corporation tax now at 25%, profit retained after tax is lower, making the $1.5 million harder to fund internally. [app] High upfront costs must be recovered through higher output, so the automated lines need to run at high capacity for years. [an] Problem 2: Automation would cut the need for 30 assembly workers, causing possible redundancies and lower morale among the remaining 210 workers. [k] Cutting jobs could damage Harwick's reputation as a stable employer in the 6 countries where it sells. [app] Low morale and industrial relations problems could disrupt production and offset the wage savings from automation. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the capital cost/cash flow risk of $1.5 million or funding difficulty
Identifies redundancies/low morale/reputation risk from automation
application_max_2: References the $1.5 million cost or the 25% corporation tax (reduced retained profit)
References the 30 assembly workers, 210 workers or 6 countries
analysis_max_2: Explains how upfront costs must be recovered through high utilisation
Explains how job losses/morale problems can offset automation savings

questions.question_text: Do you think Harwick Appliances Ltd should automate the 2 production lines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: automating solves the underlying problem — near full employment means labour is scarce and Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year. [k] Harwick employs 210 workers, cannot recruit assembly staff and faces 25% corporation tax, so cutting unit labour costs protects profit. [app] The $1.5 million spent on 2 lines would stabilise output of washing machines and ovens and remove the 30 hard-to-fill vacancies. [an] However, $1.5 million is a major commitment and automating may cut jobs and lower morale among the workforce. [k] Keeping manual lines preserves all 210 jobs and avoids upfront debt, but slower output and rising wages would hold Harwick back while revenue grows from $16.1 million to $18.5 million. [app] Redundancies could also hurt the brand's reputation in 6 markets, though retraining affected workers onto the new lines would soften this. [an] Overall, Harwick should automate the 2 lines, because chronic labour shortages near full employment make the current approach unsustainable. [eval] This is justified by 7% wage growth and the recruitment gap; spending $1.5 million now is cheaper long-term than permanent wage inflation, provided some workers are retrained. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies automation as the fix for labour scarcity/wage inflation
Identifies the job losses/morale/upfront cost risks of automation
application_max_2: References 210 workers, 7% wage rise, 25% corporation tax or the 30 assembly workers
References the $1.5 million cost, revenue growth from $16.1 million to $18.5 million or 2 production lines
analysis_max_2: Explains how automation cuts unit labour costs and stabilises output
Explains the morale/reputation risk and how retraining mitigates it
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. automate with retraining)
Weighs both options using stem figures rather than one-sided argument
